He reports that he frequently trips over his toes and drags his foot. He also gets frequent cramps when he stretches in bed in the mornings. The weakness is progressing to involve both legs now. On examination, you note tongue fasciculations. Deep tendon reflexes are 3+ at the knees and ankles. Strength is 4– at the extensors and flexors of the right foot and 4+ at the left foot. Hand grip strength is also 4+. Which of the following is the suspected pathologic lesion(s)?

options.text: Loss of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord
Loss of large pyramidal cells in the precentral gyrus
Lymphocytic infiltrate of spinal roots and nerves

explanation: This patient is presenting with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a common motor neuron disease with an incidence of 1–3 per 100,000 population and prevalence of 3–5 per 100,000 population. ALS is responsible for about 1 in 1000 deaths in North America and Western Europe. This progressive disease has no curative treatment at this time, and it leads to disability and death due to respiratory failure within 3–5 years after diagnosis. The pathologic hallmark of ALS is loss or death of both upper and lower motor neurons. The upper motor neuron loss can be demonstrated by degeneration of the corticospinal tracts typically originating in layer five of the motor cortex and descending downward via the pyramidal tract to synapse with the lower motor neurons both directly and indirectly via interneurons. The lower motor neuron disease is manifested by death of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and brainstem, which can lead to bulbar symptoms. Clinically, this leads to the classic findings of both upper and lower motor neuron disease in ALS. The most common presenting symptom in ALS is asymmetric weakness of insidious onset that is most prominent in the lower extremities. Muscle wasting and atrophy may be prominent. A detailed history can elicit cramping with volitional movements, such as stretching, which is most common in the early morning hours. Fasciculations may be identified. When the muscles of the hands are involved, extensor weakness is more common than flexor weakness. Bulbar symptoms include difficulty with chewing, swallowing, and movements of the face and tongue. Upper motor neuron symptoms may lead to spasticity with increased deep tendon reflexes. However, even in late stages of the disease, sensory and cognitive functions are preserved.
high_yield_pearl: This patient is presenting with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a common motor neuron disease with an incidence of 1–3 per 100,000 population and prevalence of 3–5 per 100,000 population.

question: You are seeing Mr. Whitacre in the clinic today. He presents with resting tremor, occasional rigidity, generalized bradykinesia, stooped posture, and gait dysfunction with frequent falls. What pathological changes would you expect to find in an autopsy specimen?

options.text: excessive CAG repeats in the HTT gene of brainstem neurons
alpha synuclein deposits in brainstem neurons

explanation: This man has symptoms of Parkinson Disease. The pathology of PD involves accumulation of alpha synuclein (Lewy Bodies) in substantia nigra neurons that leads to their death.
high_yield_pearl: This man has symptoms of Parkinson Disease. The pathology of PD involves accumulation of alpha synuclein (Lewy Bodies) in substantia nigra neurons that leads to their death.

question: A 27-year-old woman presents for neurologic evaluation after experiencing a severe burn on the palm of her right hand. She had placed her hand onto the hot surface of a smooth electric range. She did not feel the burn when it occurred and only when she picked her hand up did she notice the burn. After that, it was discovered that the patient unknowingly has bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in both hands. However, she does have touch and vibratory sense. Mapping of her loss of sensation shows decreased pain sensation in the nape of her neck, shoulders, and upper arms as well in a cape-like distribution. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the biceps and triceps, and there is visible muscle wasting of the right biceps and shoulder musculature. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Syringomyelia is a developmental disorder of the spinal cord that results in enlargement of the central cavity of the spinal cord. More than half of all cases are associated with a concomitant Chiari I malformation of the brainstem with protrusion of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum and into the cervical spinal canal. Although controversial, one theory for the pathogenesis of syringomyelia is impaired cerebrospinal fluid flow with secondary enlargement of the central spinal cord, and the common coexistence with Chiari malformations may provide support for this theory. Symptoms of syringomyelia develop gradually, often beginning in late adolescence or early adulthood. The symptoms progress irregularly and may even arrest for a prolonged period. The presentation of syringomyelia typically includes both sensory loss and muscle wasting and weakness. The sensory disturbance is dissociative with loss of pain and temperature sensation, but preservation of vibration and touch. Patients may present with injuries or burns that occur when the patient is unaware of a painful sensation in the affected limb. The distribution of sensory loss is classically described as cape-like, affecting the nape of the neck, shoulders, upper arms, and hands. Patients are areflexic in the upper limbs. Symptoms may be asymmetric. As the cavity enlarges, it can further lead to spasticity and weakness in the lower extremities as well. There are no definitive treatment options for the disease. If a Chiari malformation is also present, surgical decompression may be required. Surgeons have attempted direct decompression of the spinal canal with varied results.
high_yield_pearl: Syringomyelia is a developmental disorder of the spinal cord that results in enlargement of the central cavity of the spinal cord.

question: A 64-year-old man presents with symptoms of tremor and a generalized feeling of slowing down. His tremor bothers him most on his left side. His past medical history is significant for depression, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He is taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily, lisinopril 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. On physical examination, he has a resting tremor with presence of cogwheel rigidity. When observing his gait, you note slow, shuffling steps with difficulty maneuvering to turn around. His facial features show decreased range of emotion and appears somewhat flat. Eye movements are full. Mental status examination shows normal mentation. Which of the following is the first choice of therapy for this disorder?
explanation: This patient exhibits classic features of Parkinson disease (PD), a diagnosis made on the basis of clinical presentation. Historically, PD could be diagnosed if the patient had two of three of the following: bradykinesia, tremor, and rigidity. However, given the significant overlap of these symptoms with atypical or secondary Parkinson syndrome, the diagnosis of PD was incorrect in about 24% of cases (Table X-38). More recently, it has been determined that a more predictive trio of features is resting tremor, asymmetry, and positive response to levodopa. Imaging of the brain may show reduced uptake of striatal dopaminergic markers in the posterior putamen with sparing of the caudate nuclear on positron emission tomography or single-photon emission CT imaging. However, imaging is not required for a diagnosis of PD and is typically only performed under research settings or if there are features that would cause one to suspect an atypical Parkinson syndrome. This patient does not have features that would lead one to suspect atypical parkinsonism. He also has no medications or other clinical conditions that would lead to secondary parkinsonism. The most common causes of secondary parkinsonism include stroke, tumor, infection, exposure to toxins such as carbon monoxide, and particularly medications. The medications most likely to cause secondary parkinsonism are neuroleptic agents, including metoclopramide and chlorpromazine. Treatment of PD is typically with either levodopa-carbidopa or a dopamine agonist. Levodopa has a long history of use in PD dating to the 1960s. Levodopa is administered in combination with carbidopa to prevent peripheral conversion to dopamine and thus prevents side effects, especially nausea and vomiting. In Europe, levodopa is combined with benserazide to prevent this conversion. Levodopa is the most effective symptomatic treatment of PD. It improves motor features, quality of life, and life span as well as improving productive years of life with increased independence and employability. However, the majority of patients treated with levodopa develop motor complications with “on/off” periods, referring to fluctuations in motor responsiveness to the drug. In addition, patients may develop involuntary movements as well. Further, the duration of benefit of levodopa subsides over time to where it approaches the short half-life of the drug. Non-dopaminergic features including falling, freezing, and autonomic dysfunction are also not treated with levodopa. Many providers now prefer dopamine agonists as first-line therapy. These drugs include pramipexole, and ropinirole. While these agents do not show comparable efficacy compared with levodopa, they are associated with fewer motor complications. It should be noted that even with use of the dopamine agonists, eventual treatment with levodopa is required in most patients. Selegiline, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and Entacapone, a COMT inhibitor, are not usually used as  monotherapy. Benztropine, an anticholinergic, is not used in elderly patients due to adverse effects on memory function.
high_yield_pearl: This patient exhibits classic features of Parkinson disease (PD), a diagnosis made on the basis of clinical presentation.

question: A 24-year-old woman presents with unilateral facial weakness including inability to raise eyebrow, blink eye, or smile on the left side. No other neurologic deficits are noted. Laboratory studies including an erythrocyte sedimentation rate, Lyme titer, and angiotensin- converting enzyme level are normal. Chest x-ray is normal. Which of the following is the next most reasonable therapeutic step?

options.text: Prednisone 60 mg daily for 5 days and then tapered over 5 days
Surgical decompression of the seventh cranial nerve

explanation: Symptomatic measures for Bell’s palsy include (1) the use of paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep and prevent corneal drying, (2) artificial tears, and (3) massage of the weakened muscles. A course of glucocorticoids, given as prednisone 60–80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days, modestly shortens the recovery period and improves the functional outcome. Although large and well-controlled randomized trials found no added benefit of the antiviral agents valacyclovir (1000 mg daily for 5–7 days) or acyclovir (400 mg five times daily for 10 days) compared with glucocorticoids alone, some earlier data suggested that combination therapy with prednisone plus valacyclovir might be marginally better than prednisone alone, especially in patients with severe clinical presentations. For patients with permanent paralysis from Bell’s palsy, a number of cosmetic surgical procedures have been used to restore a relatively symmetric appearance to the face.
high_yield_pearl: Symptomatic measures for Bell’s palsy include (1) the use of paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep and prevent corneal drying, (2) artificial tears, and (3) massage of the weakened muscles.

question: A 38-year-old man presents with depression and has uncontrollable writhing movements of the extremities. His uncle died of a similar disease. What would confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Chromosomal analysis looking for CGG repeats in chromosome 4
Chromosomal analysis looking for CAG repeats in chromosome 4
Chromosomal analysis looking for CAG repeats in chromosome 8

explanation: The history is consistent with Huntington Disease.
high_yield_pearl: The history is consistent with Huntington Disease.

question: A 39-year-old handball hustler noticed the abrupt onset of involuntary movements of his right side. His right arm and leg would make large, violent, flailing movements that interfered with his game. The most likely site of damage was his
explanation: The patient has symptoms of hemiballismus. This disorder involves a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus (STN). The left STN communicates with the left GPi, left VL of thalamus, and left motor cortical area. Left motor cortex controls movements of the right side of the body via the corticospinal tract.
high_yield_pearl: The patient has symptoms of hemiballismus. This disorder involves a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus (STN).

question: The motor dysfunctions characteristic of the above disorder can best be accounted for in terms of loss of:

options.text: Excitatory input to the GPe segment
Excitatory input to the GPi segment
Excitatory input to VL of thalamus

explanation: Hemiballismus results from the death of neurons in the subthalamic nucleus (STN). STN neurons synapse on neurons of Globus Pallidus internal segment. STN has an excitatory effect on GPi that is countered by the inhibitory connection from putamen to GPi in the direct circuit.
high_yield_pearl: Hemiballismus results from the death of neurons in the subthalamic nucleus (STN).

question: An elderly male saw his physician because he was excreting large amounts of urine. He also drank extremely large amounts of water, but he was always thirsty no matter how much he drank. An MRI suggested the presence of a hypothalamic lesion. Which of the following structures was the site of this lesion?
explanation: This condition is diabetes insipidus. Lesions of the supraoptic nucleus (and PVN) affect the release of vasopressin, which under normal conditions projects to the posterior pituitary and ultimately targets the kidneys, resulting in increased water absorption in that organ. Therefore, a lesion of the supraoptic nucleus would block this mechanism and result in increased water intake because of the failure of the kidney to absorb water.
high_yield_pearl: This condition is diabetes insipidus. Lesions of the supraoptic nucleus (and PVN) affect the release of vasopressin, which under normal conditions projects to the posterior pituitary and ultimately targets the kidneys, resulting in increased water absorption in that organ.

question: A 60-year-old man with seizures complained that he was experiencing olfactory hallucinations of unpleasant smells (cacosmia). A magnetic resonance imaging scan revealed the presence of a tumor in his brain. Which of the following choices is the most likely site of the location of the tumor?
explanation: Seizures involving parts of the temporal lobe produce olfactory hallucinations of unpleasant smells (cacosmia). This condition is also referred to as an uncinate fit. Parts of the temporal lobe include the uncus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala, and piriform cortex. Uncinate fits are caused when these structures are damaged. Other structures mentioned in the question are not involved in olfaction.
high_yield_pearl: Seizures involving parts of the temporal lobe produce olfactory hallucinations of unpleasant smells (cacosmia).

question: A stapedectomy procedure was done on a 40-year-old woman who had otosclerosis in the right ear. Three weeks later, the woman experienced a constant, unpleasant metallic taste arising from the ipsilateral anterior two thirds of the tongue (dysgeusia). Which one of the following ipsilateral nerves was damaged in this patient?
explanation: Dysgeusia (constant, unpleasant, metallic taste arising from the ipsilateral anterior two thirds of the tongue) may occur if axons in the chorda tympani are stretched or damaged, but not severed, during middle ear surgery requiring reflection of the tympanic membrane or stapedectomy. The chorda tympani branches from the facial nerve (CN VII) inside the facial canal, runs through the middle ear and innervates the taste buds in the anterior third of the tongue, and carries taste sensations to the brain.
high_yield_pearl: Dysgeusia (constant, unpleasant, metallic taste arising from the ipsilateral anterior two thirds of the tongue) may occur if axons in the chorda tympani are stretched or damaged, but not severed, during middle ear surgery requiring reflection of the tympanic membrane or stapedectomy.

question: A patient had experienced continuous bouts of hyperthermia (i.e., high temperature) and was seen by a neurologist. A neurological examination suggested the presence of a hypothalamic lesion. The most likely site of the lesion was the:
explanation: The anterior hypothalamus (and preoptic region) is referred to as a heat loss region. Specialized receptors and the neurons with which they are associated in this region respond to increases in body temperature by discharging, resulting in autonomic changes such as vasodilation and perspiration, leading to a lowering of body temperature. A lesion of this region would disrupt this mechanism and would thus lead to hyperthermia. Other choices in this question include regions where this kind of mechanism is not present, and thus, they are unrelated to thermoregulation in this manner. The posterior hypothalamus is believed to be a heat conservation region where an opposing autonomic mechanism is present, leading to an elevation in body temperature when body temperature decreases below a normal level.
high_yield_pearl: The anterior hypothalamus (and preoptic region) is referred to as a heat loss region.

question: A patient presented with paralysis of the left side of the limbs and left side of the lower face, and deviation of the tongue to the left with no atrophy and with no loss of taste sensation. These deficits most likely resulted from a lesion of the:

options.text: Ventromedial medulla on the right side
Ventromedial medulla on the left side

explanation: The right internal capsule contains corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers that project to the contralateral spinal cord and to the brainstem. The corticobulbar fibers that project predominantly to the contralateral side include those fibers that innervate motor nuclei of cranial nerves (CN) VII (lower facial muscles) and XII (hypoglossal). Therefore, a lesion of the right internal capsule will result in paralysis of the limbs on the left side, a deviation of the tongue to the left side (i.e., side opposite to the lesion), and paralysis of the right side of the lower face. A lesion of the right ventromedial medulla is too far caudal to affect corticobulbar fibers that supply the facial nucleus. Because the defects are on the left side, all of the choices that involve a lesion on the same (i.e., left) side are incorrect, because lesions of the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers result in motor deficits that are manifested on the contralateral side.
high_yield_pearl: The right internal capsule contains corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers that project to the contralateral spinal cord and to the brainstem.

question: A 35-year-old man had a stroke that did not cause paralysis. However, he discovered that he was unable to perform complex learned movements. The region of the cerebral cortex most likely affected by the stroke was the:
explanation: The premotor area is extremely important in providing sequencing or programming mechanism for learned movements. The most significant inputs come from the posterior parietal cortex. The premotor cortex then signals the appropriate groups of neurons in the spinal cord (and/or brainstem) to respond in a particular set of sequences. Therefore, damage to this region would result in loss of the sequencing mechanism that is so necessary for the occurrence of complex learned movements. The resulting disorder is called apraxia. Damage to the postcentral gyrus will produce a somatosensory loss. Damage to the precentral gyrus will produce an upper motor neuron paralysis. Damage to the temporal cortex will produce an auditory loss, and damage to the prefrontal cortex will produce different kinds of intellectual deficits, none of which include apraxia.
high_yield_pearl: The premotor area is extremely important in providing sequencing or programming mechanism for learned movements.

question: During what appeared to be routine surgery for a torn ligament, a middle-aged man had a stroke. After a few days, the patient showed some recovery because he was able to walk with some difficulty and, in addition, sensory functions seemed normal. However, a neurologic evaluation revealed a weakness in muscles that regulate breathing, speech, swallowing, and facial expression. A subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan indicated that the stroke was limited but primarily affected the:

options.text: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Anterior limb of the internal capsule

explanation: The symptoms described in this case reflect pseudobulbar palsy, which is characterized by weakness in the muscles of the head and face. It involves corticobulbar pathways that innervate, in part, cranial nerve motor nuclei. These fibers are contained in the genu of the internal capsule. Damage to the premotor cortex would produce a form of apraxia. Damage to the medullary pyramids is too low to affect corticobulbar fibers, which supply the facial nerve. The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains corticospinal fibers, which have no influence on brainstem cranial nerve activity. The anterior limb of the internal capsule contains frontopontine fibers, which synapse with pontine nuclei in the basilar pons and thus constitute part of a circuit linking the cerebral and cerebellar cortices. Accordingly, this pathway is not related to functions of cranial nerve motor nuclei.
high_yield_pearl: The symptoms described in this case reflect pseudobulbar palsy, which is characterized by weakness in the muscles of the head and face.

question: A patient who displays spasticity, paralysis or weakness of limbs, increased tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on one side most likely has a lesion of the:

options.text: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
Dorsal horn of the spinal cord
Posterior limb of the internal capsule

explanation: The symptoms described in this case are that of an upper motor neuron disorder. In this question, the only possible answer is the posterior limb of the internal capsule, which contains the corticospinal tract. Lesion of the ventral horn results in a lower motor neuron disorder; the dorsal horn of spinal cord, premotor cortex, and posterior parietal cortex do not contain corticospinal fibers and therefore lesions of these regions would not produce an upper motor neuron syndrome.
high_yield_pearl: The symptoms described in this case are that of an upper motor neuron disorder.

question: A 55-year-old man saw his physician because he had been depressed for the past 6 months. As he sat in his chair the physician noticed spontaneous fidgety and jerky movements that the man made with his arms and legs. There was no tremor of his hands or slowness of movement. The man indicated that his father had similar symptoms and that he didn’t want to end his life in the same way. This disorder results in the loss of which neurotransmitter?
explanation: This man has Huntington Disease. HD causes the loss of inhibitory putamen neurons that synapse on neurons of the GPe. These inhibitory putamen neurons release GABA as the inhibitory transmitter.
high_yield_pearl: This man has Huntington Disease. HD causes the loss of inhibitory putamen neurons that synapse on neurons of the GPe.

question: The motor dysfunctions characteristic of the above disorder can best be accounted for in terms of loss of:

options.text: Inhibitory input to the caudate nucleus
Inhibitory input to the GPi segment
Inhibitory input to the GPe segment

explanation: Huntington Disease results in the death of neurons in the caudate and putamen. The putamen neurons are the ones that cause the movement abnormalities. HD specifically results in death of the putamen neurons that project in the indirect circuit. Those putamen neurons make inhibitory synapses onto neurons in GPe where they release GABA.
high_yield_pearl: Huntington Disease results in the death of neurons in the caudate and putamen.

question: A 65 year old woman was diagnosed with a hypokinetic movement disorder. She exhibited spontaneous movements in her hands as well as other symptoms. The basic mechanism that characterizes hypokinetic disorders involves:

options.text: Reduced glutamate input to the neostriatum
Increased GABA input to the GPe segment
Reduced quantities of dopamine onto the neostriatum
Reduced quantities of dopamine released into VL of thalamus
Reduced quantities of GABA released onto the neostriatum

explanation: Hypokinetic disorders, like Parkinson Disease, are characterized by slowed movements and difficulty starting movements. These disorders result from reduced release of dopamine onto putamen neurons. Putamen together with caudate nucleus are considered the neostriatum.
high_yield_pearl: Hypokinetic disorders, like Parkinson Disease, are characterized by slowed movements and difficulty starting movements.

question: A patient presents with a stroke involving Interruption of corticobulbar fibers in the left cerebral peduncle. This would result in weakness of

options.text: the left side of the face
the right side of the face
the left lower quadrant of the face
the right lower quadrant of the face
the right upper half of the face

explanation: For CN VII, motoneurons for the lower face are supplied only by contralateral corticobulbar fibers. Motoneurons for the upper face are supplied by corticobulbar fibers bilaterally, so the upper face is protected against deficits from lesions.
high_yield_pearl: For CN VII, motoneurons for the lower face are supplied only by contralateral corticobulbar fibers.

question: A patient who had a stroke has difficulty swallowing and speaks in a raspy tone. Motor neurons for the skeletal muscles controlling these functions are located in (the)

options.text: dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

explanation: Inability to swallow and raspy voice are symptoms of weakness of pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles. These muscles are supplied by motoneurons in nucleus ambiguous in the rostral medulla.
high_yield_pearl: Inability to swallow and raspy voice are symptoms of weakness of pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.

question: A caloric test was performed on a 50-year-old man who remained unconscious for several weeks after a motor vehicle accident. What response would the neurologist expect that indicated a a good outcome for the man?
explanation: In the caloric test, cool or warm water is infused into the external ear canal. The temperature differential of the water creates currents in the endolymph of the semicircular canals that stimulates their receptors. The stimulation evokes nystagmus in both eyes by activating the vestibulo-ocular pathway.
high_yield_pearl: In the caloric test, cool or warm water is infused into the external ear canal.

question: A 24-year-old woman developed seizures in which her eyes were turned to the left. What area might be involved in her seizures?
explanation: The frontal eye fields (FEF) in the frontal lobe controls lateral position of the eyes. Activity in the FEF on one side of the brain causes the eyes to turn toward the opposite direction.
high_yield_pearl: The frontal eye fields (FEF) in the frontal lobe controls lateral position of the eyes.

question: In experiments to understand control of eye movements, an investigator stimulated the right paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF/Horizontal gaze center). What effect would the stimulation have on eye position?

options.text: the left eye to move left

explanation: The PPRF controls horizontal gaze by connections with ipsilateral CN VI nucleus. Stimulation of the PPRF would cause the ipsilateral eye to move to the same side and the contralateral eye to move to that side also (through connections with the MLF and CN III nucleus). Another way to think about this is that the FEF causes eyes to turn to the opposite side – the FEF connects to the contralateral PPRF – so the PPRF causes the eyes to turn to the same side.
high_yield_pearl: The PPRF controls horizontal gaze by connections with ipsilateral CN VI nucleus.

question: A common test to determine whether an auditory deficit is due to a conduction or a sensorineural problem and to which ear is called a Weber test. In the Weber test a tuning fork, while vibrating, is placed in a midline structure of the face or skull. The sound coming from the vibration while in the midline structure will sound louder in an ear that has a conduction block and significantly reduced in an ear that has sensorineural damage. Why does the ear with a conduction block sense the vibration as being louder?

options.text: Conduction block compensates by an increase in the number of inner hair cells
Increased background noise in the unaffected ear
Sensorineural activity in both ears decreases
The outer hair cells become more active

explanation: Outside noises normally result in reflexes within the ear (CN VII and CN VIII) that reduce sounds to enhance the frequency range of human voice (approximately 5000 Hz). Conduction blockade will result in diminishing outside noises, decreasing the normal reflexes, and may sound louder (try placing a vibrating tuning fork on your head, midline, while plugging one ear and see if it sounds louder in the plugged ear).
high_yield_pearl: Outside noises normally result in reflexes within the ear (CN VII and CN VIII) that reduce sounds to enhance the frequency range of human voice (approximately 5000 Hz).

question: A patient was evaluated who had bilateral damage to the occipital lobes. Which of the following functions would be affected

question: Damage to motor cortex on one side typically causes the most contralateral weakness when

question: A 48-year-old man was admitted to a hospital for repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. During the repair of the aneurysm, blood flow in the artery of Adamkiewicz was interrupted, causing postoperative spinal cord ischemia and infarction of the lumbosacral spinal cord from T8 to L2. What deficits would have occurred due to this infarct?

options.text: paraplegia of the lower limbs with flaccid paralysis
paraplegia of the lower limbs with proximal flaccid and distal spastic paralysis
quadriplegia of all 4 limbs with spasticity and hyper-reflexia
quadriplegia of all 4 limbs with flaccid paralysis and hypo-reflexia

explanation: At the level of each vertebral segment, radicular arteries arise from neighboring arteries, which include subclavian arteries in the cervical region, intercostal arteries in the thoracic region, and lumbar and sacral arteries. The radicular arteries arising at the vertebral segments enter the spinal canal through corresponding intervertebral foramina. Large radicular arteries supply blood to both the spinal cord and nerve roots. A radicular artery, much larger than other radicular arteries, arises usually on the left side, at T9–L1 levels from the intercostal (T9–T12) or lumbar (L1) arteries. The artery enters the spinal canal through the left T9–L1 foramina, makes a hairpin curve, and ascends to T4–T6 levels where it anastomoses with the anterior spinal artery. This radicular artery is called the artery of Adamkiewicz and provides much of the blood supply to the anterior spinal artery for the lower one-third of the spinal cord. It is very important to identify the artery of Adamkiewicz in patients with thoracoabdominal or descending thoracic aortic aneurysms so that interruption of blood flow in this artery can be avoided during the repair of these aneurysms. Interruption of blood flow in the artery of Adamkiewicz during repair of thoracoabdominal or descending thoracic aortic aneurysms may cause postoperative spinal cord ischemia and infarction of lumbosacral spinal cord, resulting in paraplegia. Infarction results in anterior spinal artery syndrome. A section of the spinal cord is infarcted, resulting in death of neurons in anterior and posterior horns and interruption of tracts in the anterior half of spinal cord. Death of anterior horn neurons results in a flaccid, lower motoneuron lesion in the area of the infarct. Dermatomes below the level of infarct result in a spastic, upper motoneuron lesion due to the loss of the corticospinal tract. Thus, a bilateral flaccid paralysis would occur for dermatomes T8-L2, the area of the infarct. A bilateral spastic paralysis would occur for all dermatomes below L2 due to the loss of the corticospinal tracts.
high_yield_pearl: At the level of each vertebral segment, radicular arteries arise from neighboring arteries, which include subclavian arteries in the cervical region, intercostal arteries in the thoracic region, and lumbar and sacral arteries.

question: A 50 year-old obese, hypertensive man is brought to the ED after a sudden onset weakness on the left side of his body including both limbs. A CT shows an infarct in the medulla. Which of the following structures would cause this condition?
explanation: Weakness is a symptom of upper and lower motoneuron lesions. A lesion at the level of the medulla causing limb weakness would involve the corticospinal tract. The lateral vestibulospinal tract provides excitatory signals to extensor muscles; the reticulospinal tract provides inhibitory signals to lower motoneurons that decrease stretch reflex amplitude; the rubrospinal tract supplies motoneurons to the upper limb flexors only; corticobulbar fibers supply the cranial nerves.
high_yield_pearl: Weakness is a symptom of upper and lower motoneuron lesions.

question: A 38 year-old man sees his physician because he has had trouble chewing. Examination reveals weakness of masticatory muscles on the right side and a CT image shows a small tumor in a related CNS area. Which other symptom is this man likely to have if the lesion is in the CNS?

options.text: loss of balance, nausea, and nystagmus
loss of pain sensation from the right face
weakness of the lower face on the right
loss of tactile sensation from the right face

explanation: Motor nucleus of CN V is supplied bilaterally by corticobulbar fibers. Therefore, weakness of masticatory muscles must be due to a lesion of the trigeminal motor nucleus. The chief sensory nucleus of V is adjacent to the trigeminal motor nucleus, making it likely that it would also be damaged.
high_yield_pearl: Motor nucleus of CN V is supplied bilaterally by corticobulbar fibers.

question: A 63 year-old patient is seen in a clinic with recent onset of a resting tremor in the left hand. During a physical exam, the physician notices stiffness of the left upper limb when passively extended or flexed and a ratchety (catch and go) quality to the movement. These symptoms could be caused by a lesion in the:
explanation: This woman’s symptoms are consistent with Parkinson Disease. The catch and go quality of her upper limb movement is called cogwheeling, due to her superimposed tremor. The substantia nigra of the right hemisphere communicates with the right cortical motor areas and results in a movement deficit on the left side of the body.
high_yield_pearl: This woman’s symptoms are consistent with Parkinson Disease.
